title: What is ETL — Extract (get data from source like database/API/file), Transform (clean, filter, join, change format), Load (put into target like data warehouse/data lake) — the most common data engineering task.

s1_definition.profdef: ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load. It is the pattern where you pull data out of one or more source systems (Extract), reshape it by cleaning, filtering, joining, enriching, and converting formats (Transform), and then write the prepared result into a target system like a data warehouse or data lake (Load). ETL transforms before loading; its sibling ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the target.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India preparing its monthly statements. Extract is a clerk going to each department and copying out the raw records — card swipes from the switch, transfers from core banking, loans from the loan system. Transform is the back office cleaning those records: removing duplicates, converting every amount to rupees, matching each transaction to Rajesh's or Priya's account, and formatting dates. Load is filing the finished, clean statements into the central archive room where managers can instantly pull them. ETL is that assembly line from messy source to tidy shelf.
s1_definition.oneliner: ETL is the assembly line that pulls raw data out, cleans and reshapes it, and files it into a system others can query.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load. It is the pattern where you pull data out of one or more source systems (Extract), reshape it by cleaning, filtering, joining, enriching, and converting formats (Transform), and then write the prepared result into a target system like a data warehouse or data lake (Load). ETL transforms before loading; its sibling ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the target.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India preparing its monthly statements. Extract is a clerk going to each department and copying out the raw records — card swipes from the switch, transfers from core banking, loans from the loan system. Transform is the back office cleaning those records: removing duplicates, converting every amount to rupees, matching each transaction to Rajesh's or Priya's account, and formatting dates. Load is filing the finished, clean statements into the central archive room where managers can instantly pull them. ETL is that assembly line from messy source to tidy shelf.

**One line to remember:** ETL is the assembly line that pulls raw data out, cleans and reshapes it, and files it into a system others can query.

sections.s2_technical:
Extract is about reliably reading data from sources without disturbing them. Sources vary: a production database read via JDBC or change-data-capture, a REST API, a message stream, or flat files. A key senior concern is extracting incrementally rather than re-reading everything each run. For example, you only pull transactions newer than the last watermark: `SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE created_at > ?` with the last loaded timestamp bound as the parameter, which keeps the extract cheap and avoids re-processing old rows.

Transform is where most of the real logic lives. You clean nulls and bad values, filter out irrelevant rows, deduplicate, join to reference data (attaching the account holder's name to each transaction), convert types and formats, standardize currency and time zones, and compute derived fields and aggregates. In Java a filtering transform looks like `records.stream().filter(r -> r.getAmount().compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0).map(this::normalizeCurrency).toList()`, where `normalizeCurrency` converts every amount to rupees. All money math uses `BigDecimal` because floating point would corrupt financial totals.

Load is writing the transformed data into the target. Senior concerns here are idempotency and load strategy: a full load replaces everything, an incremental append adds new rows, and an upsert (merge) inserts new keys and updates existing ones so re-running does not create duplicates. You also decide batch size and transaction boundaries so a failure does not leave the target half-written.

The distinction between ETL and ELT matters. Classic ETL transforms in a separate processing layer before loading, which suits strict schemas and when the target is expensive compute. ELT loads raw data into a powerful warehouse or lake first, then transforms using the target's engine, which suits modern cloud warehouses with cheap storage and elastic compute. A senior data engineer also wraps ETL in orchestration (Airflow) for scheduling, dependencies, and retries, and adds data-quality checks between stages so a bad extract never silently poisons the warehouse.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores raw transactions in the core system but they only carry an account id, not the holder's name, and some rows are dirty. Analysts cannot work with that directly. This is exactly the Extract and Transform steps — we pull the raw rows and enrich them by joining to the account reference table.

Problem 2 — Re-running the nightly job must not duplicate yesterday's data in the warehouse. This is exactly the idempotent Load step using an upsert keyed by transaction id.

Problem 3 — A bad record (null amount) must never reach the warehouse. This is exactly a transform-stage data-quality filter.

The mini-project models `SourceRow` (raw extract) and `Account` (reference data for the join). `EtlJob` has `extract()` returning raw rows, `transform()` filtering bad rows and enriching each with the holder name, and `load()` upserting into an in-memory warehouse map keyed by transaction id so re-runs are safe. The demo runs the job twice to prove no duplication.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three raw source rows: TXN-1 (Rajesh, 1200), TXN-2 (Priya, 5000), and TXN-3 (Rajesh, null amount). Reference data maps SAV2001 to Rajesh Kumar and CUR3001 to Priya Sharma.

Step 1 — Extract. The job reads all three raw rows. They carry only account ids, no names, and one has a null amount. The data sits as `SourceRow` objects.

Step 2 — Transform, filter. TXN-3 has a null amount, so the data-quality filter drops it with a warning. Two rows survive.

Step 3 — Transform, enrich. For each surviving row the job looks up the account in reference data and attaches the holder name. TXN-1 becomes Rajesh Kumar, TXN-2 becomes Priya Sharma, producing two `EnrichedTransaction` records.

Step 4 — Load. The job upserts both records into the warehouse map keyed by transaction id. After run 1 the warehouse holds two rows.

Step 5 — Re-run proves idempotency. The identical job runs again. Because load uses put-by-key, TXN-1 and TXN-2 overwrite themselves rather than duplicating. The warehouse still holds exactly two rows.

```
INFO: === ETL RUN 1 ===
INFO: EXTRACT: reading raw source transactions
INFO: TRANSFORM: filtering invalid rows and enriching with holder name
WARNING: Dropping invalid row TXN-3
INFO: LOAD: upserting into warehouse (idempotent by txn id)
INFO: Warehouse now holds 2 rows
INFO: === ETL RUN 2 ===
INFO: Warehouse now holds 2 rows
INFO: TXN-1 Rajesh Kumar 1200.00
INFO: TXN-2 Priya Sharma 5000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load, and it is the most common task in data engineering. Extract is reliably reading data from source systems like databases, APIs, streams, or files without disturbing them. Transform is where most of the logic lives: cleaning nulls and bad values, filtering, deduplicating, joining to reference data to enrich records, converting types and currencies, and computing derived fields. Load is writing the prepared result into a target like a data warehouse or data lake. A sibling pattern called ELT flips the order, loading raw data first and transforming inside a powerful target, which suits modern cloud warehouses.

There are several senior concerns I always apply. For extract I pull incrementally using a watermark rather than re-reading the whole source every run, which keeps the job cheap. For transform I always do money math in BigDecimal because floating point would corrupt financial totals, and I enrich each transaction by joining to reference data. For load I care about idempotency and load strategy, choosing between full replace, append, and upsert, and I prefer an upsert keyed by a stable id so that re-running a failed job never creates duplicates. Around all of it I add orchestration with Airflow for scheduling, dependencies, and retries, and data-quality checks between stages.

In my project at the National Bank of India the nightly job pulled raw transactions that carried only an account id, filtered out dirty rows like a null amount, enriched each surviving row by joining to the account reference table to attach Rajesh's or Priya's name, and upserted the result into the warehouse keyed by transaction id. I deliberately made it safe to re-run, so even if the job ran twice the warehouse row count stayed stable. That idempotency is critical in banking, because a duplicated transaction in a report is not a cosmetic bug — it can mislead a regulator or a customer about real money.
